evidence_quotes.quote: This paper reports on intensive monitoring at seven commercial private water supplies (six of which were treated) spread throughout the UK serving hotels, holiday parks and food production enterprises.

The 140,000 UK private water supplies (PWS) (Reid et al. 2003) are regulated by the Private Water Supply Regulations (1991) (Anon 1991). These require Local Authorities to sample and analyse water with the sampling frequency determined by the type of water supply.

Seven private water supply sites were selected across the UK; two in each of England, Scotland, and Wales and one in Northern Ireland (Table 1). The sites included holiday camps, a hotel, a hospital, a farm and a small rural village with a resident population of approximately 500.

A total of 1178 samples were analysed, mostly for bacteria and protozoan parasites. The results are summarised in Tables 2 to 6. Each site was sampled on approximately 40 consecutive days over each of the two phases.

Pathogen contamination of these supplies was highly episodic and the regulatory monitoring system employing relatively infrequent faecal indicator enumeration (e.g. class D Category 1 supplies (25 to 100 persons) sampled once per year) would be unlikely to characterise risks from this pattern of contamination.

criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1: The study investigates microbiological water quality (bacterial faecal indicators, bacterial pathogens, protozoan parasites and viruses) across seven commercial private water supplies (holiday camps, a hotel, a hospital, a farm and one small rural village). It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability or affordability, falling directly under Exclusion Criterion 3 (water-quality studies that do not examine access or governance).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails C2 under both readings. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper mentions the UK Private Water Supply Regulations (1991) as background context, evaluates sample failure rates against statutory microbiological drinking-water standards, and argues in discussion that infrequent statutory faecal-indicator sampling misses episodic contamination; it does not empirically test a legal, institutional or governance exposure variable (and even if regulatory compliance thresholds were treated as satisfying broad C2, the paper still fails C1 and C4). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it clearly fails because it examines no rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement governing access or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing service access).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3: Empirical longitudinal environmental/microbiological monitoring study analysing 1,178 daily water samples collected over two six-week periods in spring and autumn 2000 alongside UK Meteorological Office daily rainfall records.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4: Reported outcomes are exclusively microbiological water-quality parameters (concentrations and regulatory standard failure percentages for coliforms, E. coli, enterococci, Clostridium perfringens, Campylobacter, E. coli O157:H7, Cryptosporidium, Giardia and enteroviruses). No outcomes related to service access, connection, availability, continuity, quantity, affordability or exclusion are measured.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies C5: Population/unit of analysis (seven UK commercial Category 2 private water supplies; 1,178 daily tap/filter water samples), environmental/technical exposures (24-hour antecedent rainfall, source hydrology and water treatment type, including before/after installation of filtration and chlorination at site 7), microbiological outcomes and longitudinal monitoring study design are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Observational longitudinal water-quality monitoring study (daily time-series sampling over two six-week periods with Spearman rank correlation against rainfall and pre/post Mann-Whitney U comparison of treatment installation at one site)
population_and_sample: Seven large commercial (Category 2) private water supplies in the United Kingdom (two each in England, Scotland and Wales, and one in Northern Ireland: holiday camps, a hotel, a hospital, a farm and a rural village of ~500 residents); unit of analysis is the water supply site / daily water sample (1,178 samples collected across two six-week phases in spring and autumn 2000)
exposure: Daily antecedent rainfall (24-hour UK Meteorological Office rain-gauge totals), water source type (borehole, well, reservoir, spring-fed stream, karst underground stream) and treatment system (including pre/post filtration and chlorination installation at site 7)
outcome: Microbiological water quality at the consumer tap: counts and statutory water-quality standard failure rates for coliforms, E. coli, enterococci, Clostridium perfringens, Campylobacter spp., E. coli O157:H7, Cryptosporidium oocysts, Giardia cysts and enteroviruses
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; per Exclusion Criterion 3, water-quality studies that do not examine access or governance). The study is an environmental microbiology and hydrological contamination study measuring bacterial indicators, protozoan parasites and viruses in seven UK commercial private water supplies in relation to rainfall and physical water treatment. It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (C1 = no), does not analyse a legal or administrative rule-type mechanism governing service access under either the narrow or plain reading (C2 = no), and reports only microbiological water-quality outcomes rather than service-access outcomes (C4 = no).
